title: Treasury Drops Venezuela From Outbound Investment Restriction List in New Proposal
excerpt: Proposed COINS Act rules keep China, Russia, Cuba, Iran and North Korea as countries of concern, ban AI deals, and open comments through December 7.
body:
• The US Treasury on October 22 proposed outbound investment rules that drop Venezuela from the list of countries of concern, while keeping China, Russia, Cuba, Iran and North Korea.
  • The rules implement the COINS Act of 2025: US investors must notify Treasury of deals in six sensitive sectors and face an outright ban on AI investments in listed countries.
  • Treasury said Venezuela was removed because the Maduro government 'no longer exists' after his capture in January; the current government led by Delcy Rodriguez does not meet the statutory definition.
  • Investors can comment until December 7; exemptions cover publicly traded securities and deals under $50,000, and firms can seek national-interest exemptions.

The US Treasury Department on Thursday proposed new rules for screening American investment abroad that remove Venezuela from the list of countries facing outbound restrictions, according to Reuters. The proposal keeps restrictions focused on China, Russia and other listed countries, and sets a public comment period through December 7.

Treasury said it dropped Venezuela because the government of former president Nicolas Maduro "no longer exists" following his capture by US forces in January. The current government, led by Maduro's deputy Delcy Rodriguez, did not meet the definition in the law, Treasury said. It added that the proposed rule could still apply to certain investments in Venezuelan entities, without elaborating.

How the outbound investment mechanism works

The system is not a general ban on foreign investment. It is a targeted screening regime run by Treasury's investment security office. US firms and individuals must notify Treasury about certain investments in entities linked to a country of concern that work in sensitive, dual-use technologies — and some investments are prohibited outright.

The legal path matters. The program began under former President Joe Biden in 2023 as an executive-order regime focused initially on China alone. Congress then passed the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025, known as the COINS Act, in December as part of defence legislation. A legal analysis by Morrison Foerster notes the COINS Act put the program on a statutory footing and expanded it beyond China (including Hong Kong and Macau) to Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba and Venezuela under Maduro, with implementing regulations still required before the expanded version fully takes effect.

"It's not just about the investment itself; it's not just about the money. It's about the network, the supply chain, and things like that that come from that investment."

— Chris Pilkerton, Treasury Assistant Secretary for Investment Security, to Reuters

What the proposal covers

Reuters reported the proposed rules require notification for prospective investments in six sectors across five designated countries, while banning AI investments outright. The six sectors are the five named in the legislation — advanced semiconductors and microelectronics; artificial intelligence systems; quantum information technologies; high-performance computing and supercomputing; and hypersonic systems — plus biotechnology, which Treasury added on its own authority.

Treasury said certain advanced biotechnologies could pose an acute risk, citing biological weapons proliferation, brain-computer interfaces and supply chain security. It said the rules do not include potential licensing agreements by US pharmaceutical companies with China, meeting a key demand of major drugmakers.

There are carve-outs. The proposal allows exceptions for investments in publicly traded companies and for transactions valued at less than $50,000, and it allows investors to request an exemption for a transaction deemed to be in the national interest of the United States.

Why Venezuela changed — and what did not

The COINS Act text listed Venezuela specifically as Venezuela "under the regime of Nicolas Maduro." That wording gave Treasury a narrow question to answer in rulemaking: does that regime still exist? Treasury answered no. That is different from a broader normalisation of investment in Venezuela — separate sanctions, export controls and anti-money-laundering rules still apply, and Treasury explicitly left open that some Venezuelan entities could still be covered.

Enforcement is already real under the existing China-focused rule. Morrison Foerster noted Treasury imposed its first civil penalty under the program on October 7 — $200,000 on Amidi, LLC for failing to notify Treasury of a roughly $92,478 investment by a controlled foreign subsidiary in a private Chinese AI company. Penalties under the current rule can reach the greater of $377,700 per violation or twice the transaction value, and Treasury can compel divestment.

What investors should do next

US investors with exposure to the five remaining countries of concern in semiconductors, AI, quantum, supercomputing, hypersonics or biotechnology should map deals against the proposal now, rather than waiting for the final rule. Comments are due December 7. For Venezuela-linked deals, the removal from this specific outbound list reduces one layer of notification and prohibition risk, but it does not clear a transaction on its own — firms still need to check sanctions lists and sector rules before committing capital.
